archetype.name: Game Manager (short-area distributor)
archetype.definition: A quarterback on a defense-first winning team who is asked to keep the ball moving horizontally, avoid sacks and turnovers, and cash in red-zone trips rather than drive the offense downfield.

report.headline: A winning record built on defense masks a passing game stuck behind the sticks.
report.take:
Bo Nix has never been a yards-per-attempt quarterback. His YPA was 6.66 as a rookie and 6.42 last year, both in the bottom third. He still posted positive EPA per play both seasons (0.089, then 0.105) because the rest of his game covered for it: plenty of touchdowns, a respectable completion rate and real production with his legs. Three years in, the frame is the same, but the parts that made it work have thinned out. His 5.55 YPA ranks 42nd of 45. His -0.076 EPA per dropback sits well below the league's 0.034. He is running for 6.2 yards a game after 20.9 last year.

The pass game has gone horizontal, and that is the source of the problem. He has thrown 54 passes at or behind the line, and those plays have cost the offense 14.1 EPA, more than the whole season's passing deficit. Passes of 0-9 air yards have been fine at +0.091 a play with a +2.7 CPOE. His average intended air distance is 5.76 yards, 3.19 yards short of the sticks on average, and his aggressiveness has fallen every season to 9.52%. That shows up on third down, where he is at -0.44 EPA per play and converts 26.2% facing an average 7.5 yards to go. Sean Payton's offense passes more than the situation predicts (+0.7, 10th), so this is not a run-first team hiding him. The volume is there; the yards per throw are not. The 4-2 record belongs mostly to a defense that ranks 3rd against the pass.

The season line is harsher than his typical week. The Week 1 loss at Kansas City (-14.4 passing EPA, four sacks) carries a lot of it. Over Weeks 2-6 his EPA per dropback is -0.003, roughly league average. One thing is clearly good: he takes few sacks (4.1%, 9th fewest) and his line allows the fewest hits in the league. The worrying part is recent. Pat Bryant, the one receiver producing big plays (+0.95 EPA per target, +12.3 total on 13 targets), went to injured reserve before Week 5. Nix then threw for 123 and 107 yards against the 9th- and 2nd-ranked defenses. Courtland Sutton has been a drain at -0.345 EPA per target.

Going forward, expect something closer to the Weeks 2-6 version than the season line: near-average efficiency, modest yardage and touchdowns supported by solid red-zone play. A soft Arizona pass defense comes next, and Bryant's projected return around November 8 should help. Getting back to his 2025 level would take more downfield throws and the running he has abandoned. Neither has shown up yet.

strengths.title: Avoids sacks and stays clean
strengths.body: He takes a sack on 4.1% of dropbacks, 9th fewest among qualifiers. His pressure-to-sack rate (17.8%) has been low in all three seasons, so this is a real trait, not a fluke. The quick, short passing diet and a line allowing the fewest hits in the league both help, and both should last. The cost is that the same get-it-out habit caps his yards per throw.

strengths.title: Short-area accuracy and red-zone finishing
strengths.body: On throws of 0-9 air yards he completes 66.7% at +2.7 CPOE and +0.091 EPA a play, with four touchdowns. Inside the 20 he has +0.229 EPA per play and all six of his passing touchdowns. He threw 29 touchdowns as a rookie, so the red-zone production fits his history. Twenty-eight red-zone plays is a small sample, but nothing about it looks lucky.

concerns.title: Third downs die short of the sticks
concerns.body: On third down he is at -0.44 EPA per play, a -26.8 EPA hole, and converts only 26.2%. That is the single biggest drag on the offense. The average 7.5 yards to go is long, but he also throws 3.19 yards short of the sticks on average. When he does push the ball 10-19 yards he has completed 40% at -14.5 CPOE with two interceptions. Third-down rates swing a lot over six games and should drift back toward his career norms. A fix needs him to attack the intermediate area, though, and so far he hasn't.

concerns.title: Screen game bleeding points
concerns.body: Fifty-four passes at or behind the line have produced -0.261 EPA a play and a 27.8% success rate. That alone costs more than his whole passing deficit. Part of it is play-calling: leaning on screens in a 28th-ranked offense by success rate. Part is execution: his CPOE on those throws is -7, unusually low for the easiest throws on the field. Unless the mix changes, his yards per attempt stays near the bottom of the league.

concerns.title: The legs have disappeared
concerns.body: He ran for 430 and 356 yards in his first two seasons. He is now down 14.8 rushing yards a game from last year. His five scrambles have cost -1.149 EPA each, and he has lost two fumbles. His designed runs are fine (+0.124 EPA), so the missing piece is the improvised scramble. No injury is listed, so this looks like a choice or a scheme change. Getting it back is the easiest route to restoring his old value.

trend.note: After a strong Week 2 (+8.4 EPA, 288 yards), his yardage has slid. He has thrown for 4.63 yards per attempt over the last three games and 123 and 107 in the two since Bryant went on IR. Those came against top-10 defenses, and his per-dropback efficiency over that stretch (-0.08) is close to his season mark.

nextGame.headline: Arizona's leaky pass defense is the softest landing spot yet.
nextGame.body:
Arizona ranks 30th in pass EPA allowed (0.271) and 30th on deep throws, where it gives up 1.213 EPA a play. It gives quarterbacks 21.6 PPR points and 2.83 touchdowns a game, both near the bottom of the league. Its short-pass defense (27th) is also poor, which matters most for a quarterback living under 10 air yards: even his usual dink-and-dunk diet should gain more than it has. The Cardinals are much better against the run (10th in rush EPA), so this looks like a game Denver wins through the air.

Arizona will be without safeties Andrew Wingard (a 76%-snap starter) and Wydett Williams Jr., thinning a back end that already gives up big plays. Denver still won't have Pat Bryant, its best downfield producer, so the deep shots this defense invites fall to Jaylen Waddle and whoever replaces Bryant. Arizona is also missing running backs Jeremiyah Love and James Conner. That weakens their offense and supports the Book making Denver a 4.5-point favorite. The risk is a big lead: with a two-score cushion he has gone conservative and posted -0.598 EPA a play on a 13-play sample. He also comes off 10 days of rest after the Thursday game.

keyMatchups.title: Waddle against a bottom-ranked WR1 defense
keyMatchups.body: Arizona has allowed 0.75 EPA per target to opposing top receivers, worst in the league. Waddle leads Denver with 39 targets but has been roughly break-even per target. If he can't produce here, the issue is the offense, not the matchup.

keyMatchups.title: Engram working the middle
keyMatchups.body: Arizona lets top tight ends score 3.5 PPR points over their usual output, 27th in the league, and sees an above-average share of targets go to tight ends. Engram has been Nix's most efficient healthy target at +0.159 EPA per target. With two safeties out, he is the logical outlet on the third downs that have sunk this offense.

keyMatchups.title: Will he take the deep shots
keyMatchups.body: Arizona allows the third-most EPA on deep passes, and Nix has been efficient on his few attempts at 20+ air yards (+0.203 on 14). He has also been reluctant, with an intended air distance of 5.76 yards. This is the game to see whether that caution is his choice or the play calls.

nextGame.watch: Whether his intended air yards rise against a depleted secondary; a game with real downfield attempts would say more than the box score.

restOfSeason.body:
Several parts of his game should hold: sack avoidance, short-area accuracy, red-zone touchdowns and a defense that keeps games close and winnable. The season-long efficiency should improve because the Week 1 disaster at Kansas City weighs heavily on it, and his Weeks 2-6 form was about league average. Third-down EPA this bad also tends to ease. His yards per attempt ranked 38th-39th in each of his first two years, so even a better version of Nix lands around 6 yards per attempt, not 7. I expect 180-225 passing yards and 1.0-1.5 passing touchdowns a game, with the low end more likely until Bryant returns.

The biggest swing is the running. Two years of 350-plus rushing yards say the ability exists, and no injury explains its absence. Even a partial return to scrambling would lift both his real and fantasy value. I project 8-18 rushing yards a game and 12-17 PPR points. Two-score leads mean low-volume, low-efficiency passing, so a dominant Denver defense trims his ceiling.
swingFactors: Pat Bryant's return from IR (projected Nov 8)
Payton loosening the screen-heavy, short-of-the-sticks play calling

confidence.note: Six games, with one outlier opener; Bryant's absence and a two-year positive-EPA track record pull in opposite directions.
